opus-5.5.text:
I think of them as complementary rather than competing. The end goal for a lot of us is a single model that goes from pixels and language straight to actions, trained end to end, because that's where you get the most generality and you avoid the brittleness of hand-designed interfaces between modules. But in practice, you rarely get there by just throwing data at a monolithic policy and hoping. Robot data is expensive and scarce, so you need the model to already be good at a lot of the intermediate things: understanding where objects are, reasoning about spatial relationships, predicting what will happen when it moves, figuring out which part of a scene matters for the task.

So improving those intermediate capabilities, things like pointing, grounding, trajectory prediction, embodied reasoning, is really about building a better foundation. When the base model has strong spatial understanding and can, say, point to where it should grasp or sketch out a rough motion path, then the action learning on top of that becomes much more data efficient. You're not asking the robot data to teach the model what a cup is or where the handle is; you're only asking it to teach the low-level control.

And the nice thing is those capabilities can often be trained on non-robot data, on web images, videos, synthetic data, which is far more abundant. Then end-to-end fine-tuning lets the model integrate all of that into behavior, and the gradients from the action objective can refine the intermediate representations too. So I see intermediate capabilities as scaffolding and as a measurable signal of progress, and end-to-end learning as the way you ultimately cash that out into robust behavior. You want both: the structure to make learning efficient, and the end-to-end training so you're not capped by the limits of whatever interface you designed.

r001.rationale: The response calls the two approaches complementary and explains that stronger intermediate capabilities make end-to-end action learning more data-efficient, while end-to-end training can refine those representations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think people sometimes frame those as opposing bets, and I actually don't see it that way. The way I think about it is that end-to-end learning is the destination, but intermediate capabilities are how you figure out whether your base model is actually learning anything useful along the way.

So concretely, if you have a robotics foundation model and you're trying to get it to do long-horizon manipulation, you want it to be able to perceive the scene, understand spatial relationships, reason about what to do next, and then actually output motor commands. If you just train end to end on robot trajectories and the policy fails, you have almost no visibility into why. Did it not see the object? Did it misjudge the grasp? Did it get the sequencing wrong? Those failures all look the same from the outside, which is the robot doing something dumb.

What we found is that if you deliberately improve the intermediate stuff, things like spatial reasoning, affordance prediction, grounding language to objects in the scene, success detection, you get a model that's much more debuggable, and more importantly, those capabilities transfer. The same visual-language backbone that can answer "which object is closer to the gripper" tends to produce better low-level policies when you fine-tune it on actions. So the intermediate capabilities aren't a detour from end-to-end learning, they're a form of pre-training for it.

There's also a data argument here. Robot action data is scarce and expensive. Internet-scale vision and language data is not. So if you can express a lot of what the robot needs to know as intermediate capabilities that can be learned from web data, or from synthetic data, or from human video, you're effectively shifting the burden off of the scarce resource. Then end-to-end fine-tuning on robot data has a much easier job because it's mostly learning the last mile, the actual embodiment specifics.

The failure mode you want to avoid is the one where you hand-design a pipeline and lock in a decomposition that turns out to be wrong. That's the classical robotics problem, you build a perception module and a planning module and a control module and the interfaces between them become the bottleneck. So the discipline I try to keep is, we improve intermediate capabilities inside a single model, with shared representations, and we evaluate them, but we never force the final policy to route through them explicitly. The model gets to use them if they help. And empirically, they do help. But the gradient still flows end to end.

So my honest answer is that it's less of a tension and more of a sequencing question. Intermediate capabilities are the scaffolding. End-to-end is the building. You don't skip the scaffolding, but you also don't confuse it for the thing you're trying to build.

r001.rationale: The response says intermediate capabilities are not a detour from end-to-end learning but a form of pre-training for it, and explains that they help the final policy.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. End-to-end learning is a way of training the system, but it doesn’t mean we should stop thinking about the capabilities that the system needs to acquire. A robot still needs to understand what it’s looking at, connect language to the physical world, and produce actions that accomplish a task.

So improving those intermediate capabilities can give you a stronger base model and make learning from robot experience more efficient. The important question is whether those improvements actually transfer to better behavior. You can get better at an intermediate benchmark without becoming better at controlling a robot.

I would keep the end-to-end task as the thing that ultimately tells us whether we’re making progress, while using intermediate capabilities to understand what’s missing and where additional training might help. You don’t necessarily need to turn each capability into a separate, hand-engineered module. You can develop those capabilities within a model that still learns jointly from observations to actions.

r001.rationale: The response says the approaches are “complementary” and explains that stronger intermediate capabilities can support end-to-end learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I see those as complementary. End-to-end learning is the direction you want to move toward, but that doesn’t mean you have to treat the model as a black box and only measure whether the robot completed the task. You still want to understand: Can it perceive the relevant objects? Can it understand the instruction? Can it reason about the spatial relationships? Can it produce the right actions?

Those intermediate capabilities give you a way to diagnose what’s limiting the system. If the robot fails because it misunderstood the scene, collecting more examples of the motion may not address the actual problem. You might get more benefit from improving the representations or the visual understanding of the base model.

But ultimately, those improvements have to translate into better behavior on the robot. An intermediate benchmark is useful insofar as it helps you build a system that succeeds at tasks. So I think there’s a productive feedback loop: use intermediate capabilities to understand and improve the model, and use end-to-end performance to test whether those improvements actually matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the approaches complementary and describes a feedback loop in which intermediate capabilities guide model improvements, while end-to-end robot performance tests whether those improvements help.
